standard_text: Graph a line given its slope and a point on the line. Find the slope of a line given its graph.

progression.narrative: This standard asks students to find the slope of a line from its graph and to graph a line given its slope and one point on it. The on-grade work moves from classifying a slope as positive, negative, zero, or undefined, to counting rise over run between lattice points, keeping the sign on falling lines, and finally reversing the process to draw a line from a slope and a point. Students who struggle here usually cannot place or read coordinates reliably, or cannot form and reduce the rise over run ratio. Intervention should start with the grade 3 to 5 foundations, plotting in the first quadrant and writing fractions in simplest form, then rebuild the grade six skills of graphing in all four quadrants and finding unit rates, and only then return to slope itself.

steps.rationale: Before computing a value, students must read a line's orientation: positive (rising), negative (falling), zero (horizontal), or undefined (vertical). Settling direction first prevents the sign errors that plague slope calculation later.

The core reading move: pick two lattice points on a graph, count rise and run, and write slope as rise over run. Kept to positive whole-number points so the only new demand is forming the ratio right-side up.
The same reading move extended to integer coordinates and falling lines, where the slope is negative. The spec explicitly allows negative slopes; the new trap is dropping the sign.
The standard's other half: reverse the machine. Plot the given point, then use the slope's rise and run to step to a second point and draw the line -- honoring the sign for a negative slope.
An Above-proficiency extension: given a slope and one point, generate OTHER points on the same line by stepping forward and backward. Proves students can use slope, not just measure it.

The Above-proficiency synthesis: read a slope straight out of a real-world rate as vertical change over horizontal change, then express and reduce it as a fraction. Connects slope to proportional rate.

skills.name: Plot and read points in the first quadrant of a coordinate grid

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point (x, y) with whole-number coordinates in the first quadrant and read a marked point's coordinates.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: To plot the point (3, 5), how far do you go across, and how far up?

skills.i_do_script: A grid point is an address made of two moves from the corner (0, 0), and the order never changes: across first, then up. Watch (3, 5): I start at the origin, walk RIGHT 3 along the bottom, then climb UP 5. The first number is always the across move on the x-axis; the second is always the up move on the y-axis. To read a marked point I reverse it: count how far across it sits, then how far up. Right 3 then up 5 and right 5 then up 3 land on two different spots, so the order is the whole game.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses the coordinates, going up by the first number and across by the second
canonical_error.example: Plots (3, 5) by going up 3 and right 5, landing on (5, 3) instead
canonical_error.why: The student forgets the fixed order. The first number is always the across move; the second is always the up move.

skills.item_template: Plot a given ordered pair or read a marked point's coordinates. Whole numbers only, first quadrant only. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: To plot (3, 5), how far do you go across, and how far up?
A point is 2 across and 6 up from the origin. Write its coordinates.
In the ordered pair (4, 1), which number is the x-coordinate?
Which coordinate tells you how far to go up, the first or the second?
Describe the moves to plot (6, 2).
A point is 7 across and 0 up. Write its coordinates.
Where is the point (0, 4)?
sample_items.answer: On the y-axis, 4 up from the origin

sample_items.stem: What are the coordinates of the origin?

redirect_script.stop: Which number is the across number?
redirect_script.prompt: Always across first, then up. Put your finger on (0, 0), walk right by the first number, then climb up by the second. Say 'across, then up' as you move.
redirect_script.praise: You went across first and up second, that is exactly the order.

vocabulary.definition: Two numbers (x, y) that give a point's address: across, then up.
The corner point (0, 0) where the x-axis and y-axis meet.
The number line that runs across the bottom of the grid.
The number line that runs up the side of the grid.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 5 first-quadrant graphing with a labeled grid: walk the across move on the floor line first, then the up move.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a first-quadrant grid from 0 to 8 on each axis. Mark two spots: right 3 then up 5, and right 5 then up 3. Label them A and B.
A and B are different spots. Which one is the point (3, 5)?
A is (3, 5): across 3 first, then up 5. The first number is always the across move, so the order of the moves decides which spot you land on.
If a student picks B, ask which number they walked across. The across number must be the first one.
Your turn: plot (2, 6), then read back the coordinates of the point you marked.

skills.name: Find equivalent fractions and write a fraction in simplest form

prerequisite_skill.description: Recognize and generate equivalent fractions and write a fraction in simplest form.

skills.i_do_script: Two fractions are equivalent when they cover the same amount with different sized pieces. Watch 6/8 on a fraction strip: 6 of the 8 pieces are shaded. If I glue the pieces into pairs, the same shading is 3 of 4 bigger pieces, so 6/8 = 3/4. On paper that gluing is dividing top and bottom by the same number: 6 divided by 2 is 3, and 8 divided by 2 is 4, so 6/8 = 3/4. A fraction is in simplest form when no number bigger than 1 divides both the top and the bottom.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides only one part of the fraction, or subtracts instead of dividing
canonical_error.example: Writes 6/8 = 3/8 by halving only the top, or 6/8 = 4/6 by subtracting 2 from both
canonical_error.why: The student changes the amount instead of renaming it. To keep the same amount, top and bottom must be divided by the same number.

skills.item_template: One fraction to simplify, or an equivalent-fraction pair to complete or check. Denominators up to 12, clean divisors. Short response fluency bank.

sample_items.stem: Write 6/8 in simplest form.
Write 2/4 in simplest form.
Fill in the blank: 1/2 = ?/6
Write 4/12 in simplest form.
Is 4/6 equivalent to 2/3? How do you know?
sample_items.answer: Yes, divide top and bottom of 4/6 by 2

sample_items.stem: Write 8/12 in simplest form.
Fill in the blank: 2/5 = 4/?
Which fraction is equivalent to 3/4: 6/8 or 4/5?

redirect_script.stop: What did you do to the top, and what did you do to the bottom?
redirect_script.prompt: To rename a fraction you must divide the top and the bottom by the same number. Find a number that goes into both, divide both, and check whether an even bigger number still divides both.
redirect_script.praise: You divided top and bottom by the same number, so the amount never changed.

vocabulary.definition: Fractions that name the same amount with different sized pieces, like 6/8 and 3/4.
A fraction whose top and bottom share no divisor bigger than 1.

next_steps.if_fail: Review grade 4 equivalent fractions with fraction strips or an area model: same shading, bigger pieces.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a strip cut into 8 equal pieces and shade 6. Below it, draw a same-length strip cut into 4 pieces and shade until the shading lines up.
How many of the 4 big pieces are shaded? Is the shaded amount the same on both strips?
3 of the 4 big pieces match the shading exactly, so 6/8 = 3/4. Dividing the top and bottom by 2 is the same as gluing the pieces into pairs.
If a student writes 3/8, point at the strips: did the bottom strip still have 8 pieces after the gluing?
Your turn: use the strips to write 4/12 in simplest form.

skills.name: Plot and read ordered pairs in all four quadrants

prerequisite_skill.description: Plot a point with integer coordinates in any quadrant and read a marked point's coordinates, using negative numbers for left and down moves.

skills.i_do_script: In grade six the grid grows in every direction, and the signs steer the moves. The order never changes, x first and y second, but now a negative x means LEFT and a negative y means DOWN. Watch (-3, 2): start at the origin, go left 3 because the x is negative, then up 2. For (4, -1): right 4, then down 1. To read a marked point I reverse it: left or right gives the x with its sign, up or down gives the y with its sign. The two signs together also name the quadrant the point sits in.

canonical_error.pattern: Ignores a negative sign and moves right or up instead of left or down
canonical_error.example: Plots (-3, 2) by going right 3 and up 2, landing on (3, 2)
canonical_error.why: The student keeps the grade 5 habit that every move is right or up. The sign is part of the direction: negative x is left, negative y is down.

skills.item_template: Plot a given ordered pair with integer coordinates, read a marked point, or name a point's quadrant. All four quadrants. Short or MC response.

sample_items.stem: Describe the moves to plot (-3, 2).
A point is 4 to the left and 1 down from the origin. Write its coordinates.
Describe the moves to plot (5, -2).
Which quadrant holds the point (-2, 5)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: Negative x and positive y is upper left, Quadrant II. 'Quadrant I' ignores the negative x; 'Quadrant IV' swaps the two signs.

sample_items.stem: A point is 3 to the right and 4 down. Write its coordinates.
Which point sits on the x-axis?
sample_items.distractor_logic: On the x-axis the y-coordinate is 0. '(0, 5)' is on the y-axis; the others are off both axes.

sample_items.stem: Write the coordinates of the point 2 left and 6 up from the origin.
In which quadrant are both coordinates negative?

redirect_script.stop: What does the negative sign tell you to do?
redirect_script.prompt: The order is still x first, then y, but the sign steers each move: positive x right, negative x left, positive y up, negative y down. Say the direction out loud before you move.
redirect_script.praise: You let the sign steer the move, left for negative x, and landed exactly right.

vocabulary.definition: One of the four regions the axes cut the plane into, numbered I to IV counterclockwise from the upper right.
Coordinates that are positive or negative whole numbers or zero.
The point (0, 0) where the axes cross; every plot starts there.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a full four-quadrant grid from -5 to 5 on both axes. Trace the walk for (-3, 2): from the origin step LEFT 3, then UP 2, and mark the point.
Why did we go left instead of right? Which quadrant did we land in?
The x is -3, and a negative x means left. Up 2 for the positive y. Left and up is the upper left region, Quadrant II.
If a student walks right 3, ask what the sign on the 3 says. The sign is the direction.
Your turn: plot (4, -1), name its quadrant, then read back its coordinates.

practice_problems.stem: Describe the moves to plot (2, 3).
In an ordered pair, which coordinate controls up and down?
Describe the moves to plot (-4, 3), and name its quadrant.
A point is 2 left and 4 up from the origin. Write its coordinates.
Which quadrant holds (-3, -5)?
Where is the point (0, -3)?
practice_problems.answer: On the y-axis, 3 below the origin

practice_problems.stem: The point (3, -2) is reflected straight across the x-axis. What are the new coordinates?
practice_problems.answer: (3, 2); the across move stays, the up-down move flips sign

practice_problems.stem: Kira plotted (2, -5) by going down 2 and right 5. Find her mistake and fix it.
practice_problems.answer: She swapped the moves. The first number is the across move: right 2, then down 5, landing at (2, -5).

activities.title: Walk the Grid
materials: Large four-quadrant grid drawn on paper or tape on the floor
A counter or marker per pair
activities.instructions:
1. Place the counter on the origin.
2. Draw a card like (-3, 2). Before moving, say the walk out loud: left 3, up 2.
3. Walk the counter, mark the point, and name the quadrant.
4. Partner reads the marked point back as coordinates to check.
5. Repeat for 6 cards, at least one in each quadrant and one on an axis. Say each time: x steers across, y steers up or down, the sign is the direction.

activities.title: Point Address Match
materials: Card deck: one card per ordered pair, one card per walk description
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each ordered pair like (-4, 1) to its walk like left 4, up 1.
3. To claim a match, name the quadrant or axis the point lands on.
4. Two decoy walk cards swap the moves; set them aside and say what pair they actually plot.

pairs.right: left 5, no up or down move

strategy_links.why: Physically walking the two moves on a floor or table grid makes the order and the signed directions concrete before any rule is stated.
The swapped-moves and dropped-sign errors are stable and predictable; finding and fixing them in worked plots confronts both directly.
Saying the walk out loud, left 3 then up 2, makes the invisible choice of direction audible and checkable.

questioning_prompts: Which number is the across move, and what does its sign tell you?
Before you move, say the walk out loud. Which direction first?
Which quadrant will this point land in? How do the two signs tell you?
What is true about every point on the x-axis?
If both coordinates were positive instead, where would the point be?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student ignores a negative sign and moves right or up anyway.
misconception_redirects.say: The sign is the direction. Negative x means left, negative y means down. Say the direction before you step.
misconception_redirects.praise: You read the sign as a direction, that is the grade six upgrade.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps the moves, going up by x and across by y.
misconception_redirects.say: Across always comes first. Put your finger on the first number and say across, then the second and say up or down.
misconception_redirects.praise: Across first, then up or down. You kept the order.

quick_checks.look_for: Left 2, down 3, landing in Quadrant III. Right or up moves mean a dropped sign.

quick_checks.prompt: What are the coordinates of a point 5 right and 3 down?
quick_checks.look_for: (5, -3), with the negative on the y, not the x.

worked_solution.stem: Plot the point (-3, 4). Describe each move and name the quadrant.

steps.annotation: Every plot starts where the axes cross.
The first number is the across move; the negative sign means left.
The second number is the vertical move; positive means up.
Negative x with positive y is the upper left region.

faded_example.stem: Plot the point (2, -5). Describe each move and name the quadrant.

steps.annotation: Every plot starts at the origin.
Positive x means right.
Use the y-coordinate and its sign to make the vertical move.
Name the quadrant from the two signs.

sentence_starters: The x is ___, so I move ___ (left/right) by ___.
The y is ___, so I move ___ (up/down) by ___.
The signs are ___ and ___, so the point is in Quadrant ___.

skills.name: Write a rate comparing two quantities and find the unit rate

prerequisite_skill.description: Write a rate as a fraction comparing two quantities and divide to find the unit rate.
prerequisite_skill.check_question: A car travels 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. How many miles per hour is that?

skills.i_do_script: A rate compares two different quantities, and the unit rate tells how much of the first for exactly ONE of the second. Watch: 120 miles in 3 hours. I write the rate as a fraction, 120 miles / 3 hours, with the quantity I am measuring on top. To get the unit rate I divide: 120 / 3 = 40, so 40 miles per hour, 40 miles for each 1 hour. On a double number line, 3 hours lines up with 120 miles, so 1 hour lines up with 40 miles. Per always means for one, and for one means divide.

canonical_error.pattern: Divides in the wrong order, putting the wrong quantity on top
canonical_error.example: For 120 miles in 3 hours writes 3 / 120 = 1/40 and calls it 1/40 mile per hour
canonical_error.why: The student divides the two numbers in the order they appear instead of asking what per what. Miles per hour means miles on top, divided by hours.

skills.item_template: A rate of two whole-number quantities. Student writes the rate as a fraction and finds the unit rate, as a whole number, money amount, or simple fraction with denominator 2, 3, 4, or 5. Short or MC response.

sample_items.stem: A car travels 120 miles in 3 hours at a steady speed. How many miles per hour?
6 notebooks cost $18. What is the cost per notebook?
A runner goes 3 laps in 12 minutes at a steady pace. How many minutes per lap?
A printer prints 90 pages in 5 minutes. What is the unit rate in pages per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 90 / 5 = 18 pages each minute. '1/18' divides in the wrong order; '85' subtracts; '450' multiplies.

sample_items.stem: A recipe uses 8 cups of flour for 4 batches. How many cups per batch?
A mail carrier delivers to 20 houses every 15 minutes at a constant rate. How many houses per minute?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 20 / 15 = 4/3 houses each minute. '3/4' divides in the wrong order; '5' subtracts; '300' multiplies.

sample_items.stem: $20 buys 5 pounds of apples. What is the price per pound?
A faucet fills 9 gallons in 6 minutes. How many gallons per minute? Write the answer in simplest form.

redirect_script.stop: What per what? Which quantity goes on top?
redirect_script.prompt: Say the unit first: miles PER hour means miles on top, divided by hours. Write the rate as a fraction with the asked-for quantity on top, then divide to get the amount for one.
redirect_script.praise: You put the asked-for quantity on top and divided, so your rate says how much for one.

vocabulary.definition: A comparison of two different quantities, like 120 miles in 3 hours.
How much of one quantity for exactly one of the other, like 40 miles per 1 hour.
For each one; the word that tells you which quantity goes on top.

worked_example_script.text: Draw a double number line: hours on the bottom marked 0, 1, 2, 3; miles on top with 120 above the 3.
If 3 hours lines up with 120 miles, what should line up with 1 hour?
Cut 120 into 3 equal jumps: 120 / 3 = 40. So 1 hour lines up with 40 miles, and the unit rate is 40 miles per hour.
If a student writes 3 / 120, ask what per what: miles per hour puts miles on top.
Your turn: use a double number line to find the cost per notebook when 6 notebooks cost $18.

practice_problems.stem: $12 buys 4 pens. What is the cost per pen?
A bus travels 60 miles in 2 hours. How many miles per hour?
A swimmer does 18 laps in 6 practices, the same number each practice. How many laps per practice?
A student types 150 words in 5 minutes. What is the unit rate in words per minute?
6 muffins cost $9. What is the cost per muffin?
A mail carrier delivers to 20 houses every 15 minutes. How many houses per minute? Write the answer in simplest form.
Store A sells 5 pounds of rice for $20. Store B sells 3 pounds for $15. Which store has the lower price per pound?
practice_problems.answer: Store A: 20/5 = $4 per pound beats Store B: 15/3 = $5 per pound

practice_problems.stem: Jia found the speed for 240 miles in 4 hours. Find her mistake and fix it.
shown_work: So the car goes 1/60 mile per hour.
practice_problems.answer: She divided hours by miles. Miles per hour puts miles on top: 240 / 4 = 60 miles per hour. A car covering 1/60 mile in a whole hour would barely move, so the answer also fails a sense check.

activities.title: Double Number Line Build
activities.instructions:
1. Draw a card like 120 miles in 3 hours.
2. Build the double number line: hours on the bottom 0 to 3, the total 120 above the 3.
3. Cut the top into equal jumps to find what lines up with 1 hour.
4. Write the unit rate with its label: 40 miles per hour.
5. Repeat with $18 for 6 notebooks and 20 houses in 15 minutes. Say each time: per means for one, and for one means divide.

activities.title: Rate to Unit Rate Match
materials: Card deck: one card per rate situation, one card per unit rate
activities.instructions:
1. Spread the cards face up.
2. Match each situation like 90 pages in 5 minutes to its unit rate like 18 pages per minute.
3. To claim a match, say the division out loud with the asked-for quantity on top.
4. Two decoy cards divide in the wrong order; set them aside and explain what they would actually measure.

strategy_links.why: The double number line makes 'cut the total into equal jumps to find the amount for one' visible before the divide rule is named.
Saying 'what per what' aloud before dividing makes the choice of numerator audible and catches the wrong-order division.
The wrong-order division is a stable error; analyzing a worked wrong answer like 1/60 mile per hour builds the sense check.

questioning_prompts: What per what? Which quantity is the question asking for one of?
Which number goes on top of your rate fraction, and why?
What does your answer mean for exactly one hour (or one dollar, or one lap)?
Does your unit rate pass a sense check? Is it a reasonable size?
Where does the unit rate show up on your double number line?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student divides in the wrong order and gets a tiny fraction for an obviously large rate.
misconception_redirects.say: Say the unit first: miles per hour means miles on top. Then check the size: could a car really cover 1/60 of a mile in an hour?
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched the top of the fraction to the unit you were asked for.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student adds or subtracts the two quantities instead of dividing.
misconception_redirects.say: A rate shares the total equally across the units. Put the total on a double number line and cut it into equal jumps, one jump per unit.
misconception_redirects.praise: You shared the total equally, that is what dividing does.

quick_checks.prompt: 80 pages in 4 days. How many pages per day?
quick_checks.look_for: 20 pages per day, from 80 / 4. An answer of 1/20 means wrong-order division.
$2.50 per roll, from 15 / 6, with the money on top.

worked_solution.stem: A train travels 180 miles in 3 hours at a constant speed. Find the unit rate in miles per hour.

steps.annotation: Per hour means miles on top, hours on the bottom.
Write the rate as a fraction with the asked-for quantity on top.
Divide to find the amount for one hour.
Label the answer: 60 miles for each 1 hour.

faded_example.stem: 4 pounds of apples cost $14. Find the unit rate in dollars per pound.

steps.annotation: Per pound means dollars on top, pounds on the bottom.
Write the rate fraction with dollars on top.
Divide to find the cost of one pound.
State the unit rate with its label.

sentence_starters: The question asks for ___ per ___, so ___ goes on top.
I divided ___ by ___ to find the amount for one ___.

skills.name: Classify the slope of a line as positive, negative, zero, or undefined
skills.i_do_script: Before I find a number, I read which way a line leans. Reading left to right: if it CLIMBS, the slope is positive; if it FALLS, the slope is negative; if it's FLAT (horizontal), the slope is zero; if it's straight UP-and-down (vertical), the slope is undefined. Watch a line through (0, 1) and (3, 5): as x goes right, y goes up, so it climbs -- positive. A line through (1, 3) and (5, 3) stays at y = 3 the whole way -- flat, so zero. A vertical line like x = 2 goes straight up -- undefined.

canonical_error.pattern: Swaps zero and undefined -- calls a vertical line 'zero' and a horizontal line 'undefined'
canonical_error.example: For a horizontal line through (1, 3) and (5, 3) says 'undefined,' and for the vertical line x = 2 says 'zero'
canonical_error.why: The student hears 'no slope / flat' and attaches it to the wrong picture. A FLAT (horizontal) line has slope zero (rise 0). A VERTICAL line has undefined slope (run 0, so you can't divide).

skills.item_template: A line described by two points or a graph. Student classifies the slope as positive, negative, zero, or undefined. MC.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 1) and (3, 5). Is its slope positive, negative, zero, or undefined?
sample_items.distractor_logic: As x increases the line climbs (y goes 1 to 5), so positive. 'Negative' reads it right-to-left.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (0, 5) and (4, 1). Classify its slope.
sample_items.distractor_logic: As x increases the line falls (y goes 5 to 1), so negative.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (1, 3) and (5, 3). Classify its slope.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The y-value never changes (3 to 3), so the line is horizontal: slope zero. 'Undefined' is the classic swap.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (2, 0) and (2, 6). Classify its slope.
sample_items.distractor_logic: The x-value never changes (2 to 2), so the line is vertical: slope undefined. 'Zero' is the classic swap.

redirect_script.stop: Flat like the floor, or straight up like a wall?
redirect_script.prompt: A FLAT (horizontal) line has slope ZERO -- no rise. A line straight UP-and-down (vertical) is UNDEFINED -- you can't run across it to divide. Trace the line: does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand up?
redirect_script.praise: You matched flat to zero and vertical to undefined -- that's the orientation nailed.

vocabulary.definition: A number that tells how steep a line is and which way it leans.
How quickly a line rises or falls; steeper lines have slopes farther from zero.
The slope of a vertical line; the run is 0, so slope cannot be computed.

worked_example_script.text: For each, does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand straight up?
Climbs -> positive; falls -> negative; flat (same y) -> zero; vertical (same x) -> undefined.
If a student calls the flat line 'undefined,' ask 'which one is like a floor and which is like a wall?'
Your turn: a line through (0, 4) and (5, 1) -- climbing or falling? What sign?

practice_problems.stem: A line climbs from left to right. Positive or negative slope?
A perfectly flat (horizontal) line has what slope?
A line passes through (0, 5) and (4, 1). Classify its slope.
A line passes through (2, 0) and (2, 6). Classify its slope.
Dev classified a line's slope. Find and fix the mistake.
shown_work: Dev wrote: 'The x changes but y stays the same, so the slope is undefined.'
practice_problems.answer: This line is HORIZONTAL (y stays 3), so its slope is ZERO, not undefined. Dev swapped the two. Undefined is for a VERTICAL line, where x stays the same and the run is 0.

practice_problems.stem: A line passes through (0, 1) and (3, 5). Classify its slope.
Two lines: line A through (0, 0) and (2, 6); line B through (0, 6) and (2, 0). Which has positive slope and which negative? Explain.
practice_problems.answer: A is positive (climbs from 0 to 6); B is negative (falls from 6 to 0). Same steepness, opposite lean.
practice_problems.notes: Contrast a rising and falling pair.

practice_problems.stem: Describe a real object that models a line with zero slope and one with undefined slope.
practice_problems.answer: Zero slope: a flat table top or the horizon. Undefined slope: a flagpole or a wall standing straight up.
practice_problems.notes: Produce-your-own model of the two flat/vertical cases.

activities.title: Which Way Does It Lean?
materials: Card set of 12 lines (each given by two points), 4 label cards: positive / negative / zero / undefined
activities.instructions:
1. Read each line card's two points aloud.
2. Decide: does the line climb, fall, lie flat, or stand vertical?
3. Place it under positive, negative, zero, or undefined.
4. Debrief: what do you look at first to tell zero from undefined?

activities.title: Floor or Wall?
activities.instructions:
1. Read Dev's claim that (1, 3) and (5, 3) has an undefined slope.
2. Sketch or describe the line -- is it flat or standing up?
3. Give the correct classification and say why.
4. Write a rule to tell zero from undefined.

content.error_step: Dev called a horizontal line undefined.
content.why: Same y means a flat line: slope 0. Undefined is for a vertical line (same x, run 0).

strategy_links.why: The zero/undefined swap is a precise, high-frequency error that find-and-fix names cleanly.
Think-pair-share on 'floor vs wall' surfaces the horizontal/vertical distinction for discussion.
Thinking aloud 'does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand up?' models the orientation check.

questioning_prompts: Reading left to right, does the line climb or fall?
Does the y-value change, stay the same, or does x stay the same?
Which one is like a floor (zero) and which is like a wall (undefined)?
What is the sign of the slope before you compute anything?
Could this line have a slope of exactly zero? How do you know?

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student swaps zero and undefined -- calls a vertical line zero and a horizontal line undefined.
misconception_redirects.say: A FLAT (horizontal) line has slope ZERO -- no rise. A line straight UP-and-down (vertical) is UNDEFINED -- you can't run across it to divide. Trace the line: does it climb, fall, lie flat, or stand up?
misconception_redirects.praise: You matched flat to zero and vertical to undefined -- that's the orientation nailed.

misconception_redirects.if_you_see: Student calls a falling line positive (reads the graph right-to-left).

skills.name: Find the slope of a line from its graph using rise over run
skills.i_do_script: Slope from a graph is a counting job: draw a staircase step between two points the line passes through and count grid squares -- squares UP is the rise, squares ACROSS is the run, and slope = rise / run. skills.name: Find the slope of a line from its graph, including negative slopes
skills.i_do_script: Look at the line before computing anything: through (0, 6) and (3, 0) it slides DOWNHILL as you walk left to right. Downhill has to show up in the number -- a positive slope belongs to a line that climbs, and this one doesn't. Slope is still rise over run, but now the line may FALL and the points may be negative -- so I have to keep the sign. Watch a line through (0, 5) and (2, 1): reading left to right the y goes DOWN from 5 to 1, so the rise is -4; the run is +2. Slope = -4 / 2 = -2. The negative says 'falling.' Watch the subtraction order too: rise = y2 - y1 and run = x2 - x1 must use the SAME two points in the same order.

skills.name: Graph a line given its slope and a point on the line
skills.i_do_script: A slope is a stair-step repeated over and over: each step goes ACROSS a little and UP a little, and slope 3 means every 1 across climbs 3 up. Flip the step -- 3 across, 1 up -- and you build a much flatter staircase, a completely different line. To graph a line from a slope and a point, I PLOT the point first, then use the slope's rise and run to step to a second point, and draw the line through both. Slope is rise / run, so a slope of 2 means rise 2, run 1: from the point go RIGHT 1 and UP 2. Watch: slope 2 through (0, 1). Plot (0, 1); go right 1, up 2 to (1, 3); draw the line. For a NEGATIVE slope like -2, the rise is down: right 1, DOWN 2. For 3/4, run 4 and rise 3: right 4, up 3.

canonical_error.pattern: Reverses rise and run when stepping, or steps up instead of down for a negative slope

canonical_error.why: The student treats the numerator as the run or ignores the sign. In slope = rise / run the numerator is the RISE (up/down) and the denominator is the RUN (across); a negative slope means the rise goes DOWN.

skills.i_do_script: A line is one stair-step copied forever: for slope 2/3 the step is 'over 3, up 2,' and walked backward it becomes 'left 3, down 2.' Any point you can reach with whole copies of that step is on the line -- any point you can't reach isn't. Given one point and the slope, I can find OTHER points on the line by stepping with the rise and run -- forward OR backward. Slope 2/3 means each right-3 step goes up 2, and each left-3 step goes down 2. Watch: line through (0, 0), slope 2/3. Forward: right 3, up 2 -> (3, 2); again -> (6, 4). Backward: left 3, down 2 -> (-3, -2). All three are on the line. To CHECK a candidate point, I make sure the rise and run from the known point reduce to the given slope.

canonical_error.pattern: Steps by the slope in the wrong direction or inverts rise/run, so the produced point is off the line
canonical_error.example: For (0, 0) with slope 2/3, picks (2, 3) (rise/run reversed) or (3, -2) (stepped down instead of up) instead of (3, 2)
canonical_error.why: The student swaps which number is the across step, or moves against the sign of the slope. A point is on the line only if (its rise) / (its run) from the known point equals the given slope.

skills.item_template: A point and a slope, with candidate points. Student selects the point(s) that lie on the same line by checking rise/run. MC or multi-select.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (2, 1) and has slope 3. Which of these points is also on the line: (3, 4), (4, 4), or (1, 0)?
sample_items.distractor_logic: From (2, 1) with slope 3: right 1, up 3 -> (3, 4). (4, 4) gives rise 3 over run 2 = 3/2; (1, 0) gives 1.

sample_items.stem: A line passes through (4, -2) and has slope -1. Which point is on the line: (5, -3) or (5, -1)?

worked_example_script.text: From (0, 0), draw the slope-2/3 step twice going forward -- over 3, up 2 to (3, 2), again to (6, 4) -- and once walked backward, to (-3, -2).
Now try to reach (2, 3) using copies of the over-3-up-2 step. Can one step, two steps, or a backward step ever land there?
Never -- (2, 3) climbs 3 in only 2 across, a steeper step than 2/3. A point sits on the line only when its rise over run from (0, 0) is exactly the slope, same value and same sign.
Write 'A line passes through (0, 0) with slope 2/3. Find two more points.'
What is one right-and-up step? What is one left-and-down step?
Right 3, up 2 -> (3, 2). Right 3 again -> (6, 4). Left 3, down 2 -> (-3, -2). All on the line.
If a student names (2, 3), ask 'is that right 3 up 2, or did you flip them?'

practice_problems.answer: Slope -1 means right 1, DOWN 1: from (4, -2) that is (5, -3), not (5, -1). Sam stepped up instead of down -- ignoring the negative sign.

activities.instructions:

skills.name: Determine the slope of a real-world linear relationship as a rate
skills.i_do_script: Put the story on the axes first: seconds run ACROSS the floor and pages climb UP the wall, so '12 pages every 8 seconds' is one point -- 8 across, 12 up. The slope is how tall the climb is compared to the walk across, and the axes decide that before word order gets a vote. In a real-world linear relationship the slope IS the rate: the vertical change (the quantity on the y-axis) over the horizontal change (the time or amount on the x-axis). Watch: a mail carrier delivers to 20 houses every 15 minutes. Houses are on the y-axis, minutes on the x-axis, so slope = vertical / horizontal = 20 / 15, which reduces to 4/3. I keep the units straight -- y-quantity on top, x-quantity on the bottom -- then reduce the fraction.

canonical_error.pattern: Inverts the rate -- puts the x-quantity (time/amount) on top instead of the y-quantity
canonical_error.example: For '20 houses every 15 minutes' writes 15 / 20 = 3/4 instead of 20 / 15 = 4/3
canonical_error.why: The student divides in the order the words appear instead of by axis. Slope is the y-axis quantity (vertical change) over the x-axis quantity (horizontal change), then reduced.

skills.item_template: A real-world constant rate described in words, with named axes. Student writes the slope as a reduced fraction (vertical change / horizontal change). Numeric response.

sample_items.stem: A mail carrier delivers to 20 houses every 15 minutes. The y-axis is houses and the x-axis is minutes. What is the slope?
sample_items.distractor_logic: 20 houses / 15 minutes = 4/3. Writing 15/20 = 3/4 inverts the rate.

sample_items.stem: A tank fills 9 liters every 6 minutes (y-axis liters, x-axis minutes). What is the slope of the line?
A runner completes 8 laps every 12 minutes (y-axis laps, x-axis minutes). What is the slope?
A store charges $10 for every 4 items (y-axis dollars, x-axis items). What is the slope?

redirect_script.stop: Which quantity is on the y-axis -- that goes on top.
redirect_script.prompt: Slope is the y-axis quantity over the x-axis quantity: vertical change on top, horizontal change on the bottom. Read the axes, not the word order. Put the y-quantity first, then reduce the fraction.
redirect_script.praise: You put the y-axis quantity over the x-axis quantity -- that's the rate as a slope.

vocabulary.definition: How much one quantity changes for each unit of another; the slope of a real-world line.
The change in the y-axis quantity (goes on top of the slope).
The change in the x-axis quantity (goes on the bottom of the slope).

next_steps.if_pass: Ready for 8.AF.4 (interpret slope as a unit rate in y = mx + b).

worked_example_script.text: Draw the axes -- x is seconds, y is pages -- and plot the printer's point: 8 across, 12 up, at (8, 12). Draw the line from (0, 0) through it.
Slope is the UP change over the ACROSS change. Looking at the point you plotted, which number is the up change -- the 12 pages or the 8 seconds?
Pages climb the y-axis, so 12 goes on top: 12 / 8 = 3/2. Writing 8/12 would put the floor distance on top of the wall climb -- the picture upside down.
Write 'A printer prints 12 pages every 8 seconds. y-axis pages, x-axis seconds. Find the slope.'
Which quantity is on the y-axis? Which is on the x-axis?

If a student writes 8/12, ask 'which quantity is vertical -- which goes on top?'

diagnostic_flow.description: Start with S3, finding a slope from a graph with the sign kept on falling lines, the At-proficiency computational core. If they pass, move up to S4 (graph a line from a slope and a point) and the extensions S5 (find other points) and S6 (slope as a real-world rate). If they fail, drop below grade level: B1 checks four-quadrant plotting and B2 checks unit rates, the two grade 6 skills slope work leans on. If those wobble, the foundations F1 (first-quadrant plotting) and F2 (equivalent fractions and simplest form) locate the gap in grades 3 to 5. S1 and S2 remain available to probe the standard's own classification and rise over run groundwork.
